title: Decision theatre or decision design?
text:
Decision theatre or decision design?

AI has made information easy, but it has not made decisions simple. As machines produce more than we can read, our job is shifting from building knowledge to owning decisions. Are we ready?

In a 2025 survey by BetterUp Labs and the Stanford Social Media Lab, 40% of US desk workers said they had received workslop in the previous month: AI-generated work that looks polished but does not move the task forward. Respondents reported spending nearly two hours, on average, dealing with each incident.

Imagine a team of ten, each receiving one piece of workslop a month. That is roughly 20 hours, more than two working days, spent cleaning up someone else’s shortcut.

We have never produced so much data, so many documents, decks and summaries. And we have never produced so much digital waste.

This is a productivity problem, but it is also a symptom.

The question is not how much faster we can produce something. It is how much extra work that production creates for everyone else, and who is left to decide what any of it means.

How did we get here?

For most of human history, change moved slowly. Roughly ten thousand years separated the birth of farming from industrialisation. Evolution had time to move from one stage to the next, across centuries and generations.

Then the interval shrank. Only about two centuries separated the first factories from the rise of service and knowledge economies.

And then it shrank again. In 1969, ARPANET connected its first computers: the beginning of the information society. Less than sixty years later, AI agents use the knowledge we put online to make recommendations and, more and more… decisions.

Think about what we did in those sixty years. We created the bits. We built digital worlds and a digital culture. We ran digitalisation programmes. We put books online with Project Gutenberg, information online with Wikipedia. We worked hard to make information accessible and ubiquitous, on every channel, for everyone.

Without knowing it, we were laying the foundation for an artificial form of intelligence to learn from our human-built infrastructure, and to work on top of it.

The information society was basically the training ground for AI. Our knowledge is now the bridge between the old, human-driven world and a new, AI-empowered one.

This compression raises a pressing question.
How quickly can people, organisations and institutions adapt?

Does more information make us wiser?

Not on its own. And we have known that for a long time.

In information management, one of the best-known frameworks is the DIKW pyramid: Data, Information, Knowledge, Wisdom. It is usually credited to Russell Ackoff, who formalised it at the end of the 1980s.

The logic is simple:

  • Data: the raw elements. Facts and signals with no context.
  • Information: data that has been processed and organised.
  • Knowledge: information that has been interpreted and put to use.
  • Wisdom: knowledge that allows judgement.

Each level is built on the one below, but the relationship only works one way. As Steyn puts it, wisdom is always knowledge, but knowledge is not always wisdom. Every level is a subset of the one beneath it.

In 1987, Milan Zeleny proposed the same four levels in a language that organisations understand much better:

  • Know-nothing: data
  • Know-what: information
  • Know-how: knowledge
  • Know-why: wisdom

Read it from the bottom up: each level is built on the one below, but no amount of data adds up to wisdom on its own.

For Zeleny, managing efficiently means knowing how to do things. Managing effectively means knowing what to do. Managing wisely means knowing why. And wisdom goes one step further: it is what lets us compare and judge our know-how and our know-what.

I first wrote about this back in 2013, on LegoViews. Back then, the challenge was getting organisations to make time for that reflection.
Today it is harder. AI hands us endless know-what and know-how in seconds, and reflection, the step that turns them into a shared know-why, is exactly the one we are tempted to skip.

Here is the point that matters most today. Wisdom comes from knowledge, but it is not a sum of knowledge.

Adding knowledge to knowledge does not make wisdom. Processing more information does not make us wiser.

What does AI know, and what doesn’t it?

AI is extraordinary at the bottom of the pyramid. It processes data at a scale no team could match, and it turns that data into know-how: summaries, drafts, analyses, code.

What it cannot settle for us is which problem deserves attention, whose interests should count, and whether we should act on its answer.

These questions depend on context. They put the output into a broader frame: what we are trying to achieve, under which constraints, and why it matters. That frame is where knowledge gets judged.

The worrying part is how many people now trust good-looking information, mistake it for wisdom, and pass it on. Especially in the domains where critical thinking is the whole job.

And even the know-how needs checking. Large language models still add unsupported claims when they summarise a document they were given. On Vectara’s hallucination leaderboard, which tests this, rates in 2026 run from 1.8% to 24.2% of summaries, depending on the model. These are task-specific figures, not universal error rates. But they show how hard it is to rely on AI output that nobody reads closely.

So we have a base of data and good-looking information, produced at a volume that no human can manage.

What are we losing?

For most of my career, the journey from data to judgement had its own pace. And it was work, real work.

We collected an adequate amount of data. We prioritised. We designed studies around sampling and around the constraints we had: time, resources, our ability to analyse, the tools at hand. The constraints forced us to choose, and choosing forced us to think.

Today we are in the middle of a data feast. We access more and more data not because we need it, but because we can.

Slowly, we are creating working conditions in which there is less room to think, prioritise, sequence and distil. Less room for intentionality.

The philosopher John Searle described intentionality as the mind’s capacity to be about something (Intentionality, 1983). In organisations, it takes a more practical shape: the deliberate decision to focus attention and action on a clearly defined purpose. What we are trying to achieve, why it matters, and how our choices serve it.

It is made of a few simple things:

  • Awareness: knowing where we are and what we are looking at.
  • Context: understanding the situation and its variables.
  • Prioritisation: directing attention to what has the most impact.
  • Distillation: separating value from noise.

Without it, we stay in the noise. We consume data because we do not know where we are going, or where we should focus.

All the narratives are about speed. We are omitting the craft.

We stopped trusting the process because we only look at the output. But an output without a process is a simulacrum: something that looks good and has no substance.

What gives value to data and knowledge is not the shape of the output. It is the process that generated it and gave it substance.

Who decides?

AI can do a lot, and it does some things better than we do. But there is one thing it cannot do: be held accountable.

The idea is much older than generative AI. A slide said to come from a 1979 IBM internal training warned that “a computer can never be held accountable”, and concluded that a computer should therefore never make a management decision. The original has never been found in IBM’s archives, but the principle has aged remarkably well (more here).

Nearly fifty years later, regulation gives human oversight a concrete organisational form. Article 26(2) of the EU AI Act asks deployers of high-risk AI systems to assign human oversight to people with the necessary competence, training and authority, and to give them the support they need.

So let’s be clear.

An insurance claim. A loan. A place at a school. Access to benefits.

AI can support every one of these decisions. It can sort the files, flag the risks, summarise the evidence. But these decisions must not become a way for organisations to hide responsibility behind a system.

These decisions affect people’s fundamental rights. Behind each one there must be a human with a name, a role, the responsibility, the authority and the skills to make the decision, stand by it, defend it, and answer for the consequences.

That does not relieve the organisation of responsibility for the system, the workflow or the conditions in which that person is expected to decide.

AI can inform. It cannot own.

This is where the paradox emerges: we have the illusion that we are outsourcing more and more work. In reality, our job is becoming that of the AI supervisor: the person in charge of making AI-enabled decisions.

In one sentence: after we digitalised knowledge and built all the infrastructure, our role is no longer only to build knowledge. It is also to take responsibility for how that knowledge informs decisions.

We are moving from the information society to an age of accountability, where we need to embrace our humanity to make decisions about other humans.

Decision theatre or decision design?

Responsible AI needs humans in the loop. That much is agreed. But a human in the loop is not enough on their own.

Put a disengaged, overloaded or alienated person in front of an AI output and you get decision theatre: the illusion that a decision happened when it did not. Someone clicked “approve”. Nobody decided.

We have a decision-making crisis, and more AI output will deepen it unless something changes. Most organisations lack a decision-making operational layer to support the people who must make the decisions.

A real decision needs three conditions:

  • Skills: the competence and training to read the context, the variables and the pre-digested input, and to tell a valid answer from a well-formatted one.
  • Authority: a name, a role and a position that allow the person to override the AI, and the responsibility to own the result.
  • Process: workflows designed to empower decision makers, with the right information, tools and time, and without drowning them in decision fatigue.

Take one away and the decision collapses into theatre.

Who holds the judgement?

It is tempting to map Zeleny’s forms of knowing onto an organisational chart: leadership decides why, management decides what, operations deliver how. But Zeleny was describing forms of knowing, not ranks of people.

The mistake is to confuse the authority to make a decision with the knowledge needed to make it well. A frontline worker may have no say in strategy, yet can be the first to notice when a process is failing or a case does not fit the rules. Research on digitalised frontline work shows that this tacit knowledge and discretion still matter, even where systems automate parts of the process.

Automate that work without asking what judgement it holds, and the organisation loses more than a task.

Imagine a caseworker reviewing benefit claims flagged by an AI system.

In the theatre version, they get hundreds of cases a day. They see a risk score and two buttons. They have no time to open the file, and overriding the system needs their manager’s sign-off. They approve what the machine suggests. On paper, a human was in the loop.

In the designed version, they get fewer cases, prioritised by uncertainty. They see the sources behind each score and the points where the system is least confident. They can override it, and they record why. Their overrides go back to the team that runs the system, so recurring problems can be investigated and corrected.

Same person. Same AI. A completely different decision.

This is where design enters the scene. Somebody has to design these decision-making workflows: to enable, and indeed empower, humans to decide, and to avoid both decision fatigue and decision theatre.

What skills will the human in the loop need?

If humans are expected to own AI-supported decisions, we need to be clear about what that responsibility requires. We need humans who think as humans, not as machines.

What does that mean?

It means humans who understand the problem, the context and the domain. It means humans who understand the AI output and the process that produced it. It means humans who can separate the validity of the content from the polish of the form.

Three families of skills will matter most.

  • Critical judgement: being sceptical, spotting errors, asking where a claim comes from, and noticing what is missing as well as what is there.
  • Sense-making: taking the knowledge we have built and organising it into structures that increase accuracy, logic, relationships and reliability.
  • Human skills: the so-called soft skills, and the hardest to delegate. Empathy for the person on the other side of the decision. The courage to disagree with the machine. The integrity to sign your name under the result.

None of these is new. What is new is that they are no longer a nice-to-have on top of the “real” work.

They are the work.

How do we teach people to decide?

If these skills are the work, we need to teach them differently. People reviewing AI-supported decisions need practice in judging incomplete evidence, recognising exceptions, understanding the context and rules that apply, and explaining what they decided and why. Without that preparation, we risk creating a new assembly line: people processing recommendations and carrying responsibility for decisions they barely have time to examine.

This means rethinking curricula, in schools, universities and workplaces, around a few plain questions:

  • How do we analyse data to tell the what from the why?
  • How do we read a situation as a system, with its relationships, feedback loops and unintended consequences?
  • How do we decide under uncertainty, and how do we stand by that decision?
  • How do we notice when we are being asked to perform a decision rather than make one?

This is why we need much more teaching in complexity theory and systems thinking. Not as niche electives for a few specialists, but as the foundation for anyone who will sign their name under an AI-enabled decision.

In one word: we need to teach judgement.

What’s next

For years, many of us watched design thinking turn into design doing: more output, faster, with less and less time to think. AI can now do the doing faster than any of us.

This is the crossroads.

One road leads to more of the same. More outputs, more workslop, more decisions that only look like decisions.

The other road brings thinking back to the centre. Framing the problem. Understanding the context. Prioritising. Designing the process that turns AI output into a decision a human can own. This is design thinking applied to the most human act of all: deciding about other humans.

References

  • Ackoff, R. L. (1989). From data to wisdom. Journal of Applied Systems Analysis, 16, 3–9.
  • Searle, J. (1983). Intentionality: An Essay in the Philosophy of Mind. Cambridge University Press.
  • Zeleny, M. (1987). Management support systems: towards integrated knowledge management. Human Systems Management, 7(1), 59–70.

Thank you for reading. I write about design, systems and the human side of AI, and I work with organisations that want to get it right. You’ll find more of my work at PatriziaBertini.com.

Author’s Note: The ideas, the research and the arguments in this piece are human — mine. I used AI to help shape the form and structure, then went through every line myself. The images are AI-generated.

title: Yes, Party Jeans Are A Thing — And These $54 Ones Are Cool-Girl Approved
text:
Yes, Party Jeans Are A Thing — And These $54 Ones Are Cool-Girl Approved

Every December, I briefly become convinced that I need a sequin dress or sparkly pants. I picture myself wearing them to a party, conveniently forgetting how many parties I actually go to and how often I end up sitting cross-legged on somebody’s couch. True Whitaker has a better idea for that particular evening. Her dream outfit for a friend’s holiday soiree includes a cashmere sweater, vintage boots, and low-rise jeans.

She’s already road-tested a version of the look, albeit on a fake plane. In Old Navy’s ’90s-inspired Jingle Jet campaign, Whitaker wore the brand’s Low Rise Baggy Wide-Leg Jeans with a sweater. “Love a perfect silhouette,” Whitaker tells Refinery29. The dark indigo is what sells me on these for a party. The wash has enough depth to sit next to your fanciest going-out tops. And the fit has the kind of slouch that makes a good sweater feel a little less proper. I’d go with a cashmere crewneck that hits right around the waistband and a pointed-toe boot that peeks out from under the wide hem. If you already own both, the jeans are the only piece you need to shop.

Whitaker shares the Jingle Jet cabin with Alan Cumming, Paris Hilton, Charli D’Amelio, Meg Stalter, Vidya Gopalan and her family, and Magic the Dog. The airplane setting also brought back memories of Whitaker’s first style icon. “My mom had the biggest influence on how I dress,” she says. “She had an incredible collection of vintage designer pieces and no matter the occasion, would serve a fit worth talking about.” Her mother wore heels on flights, a detail I thought about longer than I care to admit as someone who aspires to be that type of extra.

Whitaker has her own good heels, too. “I have a pair of dark red Prada velvet heels that I love to pull out for a good holiday party,” she says. I’d borrow that detail for a dressier take on the same outfit. Keep the jeans, swap the boots for a cheerful mood shoe, and let a sliver of color show beneath the hem. It’s just enough holiday for me, and I can guarantee those jeans would see more of January and the rest of 2027 than any sequin pants ever would.

title: Havilah Unique: From Foster Care to Creative Multi-hyphenate
text:
Havilah Unique: From Foster Care to Creative Multi-hyphenate

Havilah Unique ‪@havilah‬ is an unstoppable creative force. An entrepreneur, multidisciplinary artist, model, and content creator, Havilah has built a career chasing her creativity. From designing jewelry, furniture, and clothing (including the top she wore during our interview), Havilah’s creativity knows no bounds. But her path to becoming an entrepreneur and creative director was not easy. Growing up in North Providence, Havilah was raised in and out of the foster care system, taking on adult responsibilities at a very early age. She overcame incredible obstacles, including being raised apart from some of her siblings, meeting her father at 26, and being diagnosed with ADHD in elementary school.

During our conversation, Havilah spoke openly about how she learned to channel her symptoms into creative entrepreneurship. She was equally vulnerable about realizing she was burned out from her work, and the two-year sabbatical she took to center herself. Havilah offers us a look into how she learned to make choosing joy an intentional practice. We explore the rituals that help her feel her best, from her DIY hair and body care routines to how she prepares for a great night out. Havilah reflects on her sobriety journey, ceremonial smoking, offering us an honest look at what it takes to protect your energy while continuing to create. After meeting Brooke three years ago, the two finally sit down to talk about being archetypal Leo women, creativity, and the beauty of becoming.

title: How To Make Friends As a Busy Adult, According to OG Community-Builder Lala Romero
text:
How To Make Friends As a Busy Adult, According to OG Community-Builder Lala Romero

I really value friendship. To me, it’s the only relationship I know that gives and takes in equal measure. Friendships provide a home, a sanctuary, for us to be our fullest, messiest, and truest selves. It’s our friends who we call when we want to perrear the night away, book a trip to our motherland, or just gab and gobble down garlic bread. It’s also our friends who hold us when we’re heartbroken, drop off meds and sopita when we’re sick, and remind us of who we are when we dare to doubt ourselves in front of them.

Friendships nourish our hearts, minds, spirits, and even our bodies — and yet, unfortunately for us, we’re in the middle of a loneliness epidemic. According to the CDC, about 1 in 3 U.S. adults say they feel lonely. Meanwhile, the Pew Research Center found that nearly 1 in 5 adults don’t have any close friends. This means that millions of people are moving through their lives without connections that make them feel known, cared for, seen, heard, supported, and like they belong.

And I think this conversation about loneliness feels particularly urgent for Latinas. We’re living through a moment when so many people are carrying fear around immigration enforcement and family separation, worrying about their safety, or feeling the weight of financial stress. When you’re living with that level of anxiety, having people you can call, people who will show up, people who make you feel safe, people who you can still experience joy, laughter, and calm with, isn’t just comforting. It’s absolutely necessary. 

But how do you build that community? How do you create that home within homegirls? Especially when you’ve graduated from school, maybe work from home, are new to town, or are just a shy, timid girl who has trouble making eye contact? Maybe you do have friends, but you all live in different cities now or are transitioning into new roles as mothers or business owners that keep you, or them, busier than usual.

In a country divided, a culture starving for connection, and a time when so many of us are just trying to hold it all together, how the hell do we make friends? I’m glad you asked! In this week’s episode of Sin Vergüenza by Somos, we’re speaking with Lala Romero, founder and CEO of Bella Doña and professional community builder, about why it can feel so hard to build community as an adult, how she does it, and what it’s taught her about friendship.

text:
Your Horoscope This Week: November 15 To 21

R29 babes, welcome to the first week in November where it finally feels like things are moving forward again! With Mercury and Venus having officially ended their retrogrades in Scorpio and Libra, respectively, the second half of November is shaping up to have a considerably different flavor than the first. We’re entering the final week of Scorpio Season with greater clarity, passion, momentum, and sensitivity to what we truly want. After spending the past month and a half reviewing our values, relationships, and needs from every possible angle, we can finally start putting those realizations into practice. There’s a sense of relief in the air, even if we’re still figuring out exactly what comes next. 

As the week begins, the moon is in Aquarius, offering us a healthy dose of emotional detachment after all the deep-diving Scorpio Season has encouraged us to do. We may find it easier to look at our circumstances objectively, laugh at situations we were taking a little too seriously, or simply enjoy being in the present moment. Then, on November 17th, the moon enters sensitive Pisces, eventually harmonizing with the Scorpio Sun on the 19th. This watery energy encourages us to be more vulnerable and honest about the realizations we’ve had throughout Mercury and Venus retrograde. Now that both planets are direct, it may feel easier to express our truth with grace and sensitivity while remaining open to hearing someone else’s perspective. Conversations that once felt intimidating could become surprisingly healing, especially when we approach them with curiosity rather than assumptions. 

By the weekend, the moon enters fiery Aries just as Scorpio Season prepares to come to a close, giving us a particularly Martian burst of energy. Both Aries and Scorpio are ruled by Mars, which is currently moving through bold, expressive Leo. Translation? We may suddenly feel ready to put ourselves out there after weeks of being more introspective than usual. Maybe you finally post that photo you’ve been sitting on, experiment with a new look, tell your crush how you feel, or shoot your shot with a creative opportunity. Whatever form it takes, this weekend encourages us to embrace a little more courage, spontaneity, and visibility. We’ve spent plenty of time getting to know ourselves on a deeper level this Scorpio Season. Now it’s time to let the world see more of who we’ve become.

Aries Sun & Rising:

Aries, now that Mercury and Venus are both moving forward, you may be surprised by how much easier it feels to get people on the same page. With Mercury direct in your shared-resources realm and Venus direct in your partnership zone, the first full week of both planets moving forward is ideal for strengthening the relationships that help you thrive. Perhaps you and a romantic partner are finally figuring out how to divide responsibilities more fairly, or you’re discovering that a professional collaboration works best when everyone brings something different to the table. There’s also an opportunity to become more comfortable receiving support, whether that’s financial, emotional, or practical. You don’t always have to be the one figuring everything out, Aries. Let yourself experience what happens when other people show up for you, too. 

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, you may feel increasingly aware of how much your priorities have evolved since late October. Rather than spending another week analyzing every emotion, take advantage of the Aquarius moon early in the week to reconnect with friends, exchange ideas, and enjoy experiences that get you out of your own head. By the weekend, the moon enters your sign, giving you an extra boost of confidence and spontaneity. With your ruling planet Mars in Leo energizing your creativity and pleasure zone, this could be the perfect time to make a bold first move,  attend an exciting event, or share something you’ve been working on. End Scorpio Season by reminding yourself how good it feels to have fun, Aries. You’ve earned it.

Taurus Sun & Rising:

Taurus, your calendar may be filling up again, but this time you’re getting a lot more selective about what deserves a spot on it. With Mercury now direct in your partnership zone and your ruling planet Venus moving forward in your work and wellness realm, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring a refreshing shift in how you manage your commitments. Maybe you’re establishing better boundaries with clients, delegating tasks to a colleague, or realizing that a professional relationship could become much more productive with a few adjustments. You may also find yourself enjoying your daily routine more, especially if you’ve been experimenting with a new fitness class, co-working space, or work schedule. The goal is to create a lifestyle that actually feels good to live, Taurus. Being booked and busy is only cute when you’re enjoying yourself. 

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon highlights your career and public-image zone, making the beginning of the week especially promising for professional visibility. This could be a great time to present an idea, update your portfolio, or reach out to someone whose work you admire. Then, as the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your social life gets a boost, and you may find yourself making spontaneous plans with friends or meeting people who share your interests. By the weekend, the Aries Moon encourages you to slow down and recharge behind the scenes. You’ve got plenty of exciting things brewing, Taurus, but you don’t need to attend every function or respond to every invitation. A little JOMO (joy of missing out) might be exactly what you need before Sag Season begins.

Gemini Sun & Rising:

Gemini, your work-life balance is getting a much-needed software update, and this version might actually be worth keeping. With your ruling planet Mercury now direct in  Scorpio and Venus moving forward in Libra, the first full week of both planets being direct brings a refreshing combination of productivity and pleasure. You may notice that your relationships with coworkers are improving, that you’re getting more recognition for your contributions, or that a project you’ve been working on is finally becoming enjoyable again. Venus in your creativity and romance zone could also inspire you to bring more personality into your professional life, whether that’s pitching an unconventional idea, adding humor to your content, or connecting with colleagues outside the usual work setting. Who says being productive has to be boring, Gemini? You might accomplish more when you’re actually having fun. 

As Scorpio Season comes to a close, the Aquarius Moon at the beginning of the week activates your travel and adventure realm, making this an excellent time to explore something outside your usual routine. You could discover a fascinating podcast, sign up for a workshop, or start planning a trip that gives you something exciting to look forward to. When the moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your career takes center stage, and you may find yourself receiving attention from someone influential or feeling inspired to take on more responsibility. Then the Aries Moon over the weekend  energizes your friendship zone, making it a great time to organize a gathering or reconnect with people who bring out your adventurous side. Let curiosity lead the way. You never know which conversation could open your next door.

Cancer Sun & Rising:

Cancer, your main-character energy is making a comeback, and this time you’ve got the confidence to back it up. With Mercury now direct in your creativity and fame zone and Venus moving forward in your home realm, you may feel increasingly comfortable  sharing more of your personality with the world. Perhaps you’re ready to film that video you’ve been overthinking, submit your work to a publication, or invite friends over for a gathering that shows off your hosting skills. You could also find inspiration in your family history, childhood memories, or cultural roots and incorporate those influences into something creative. There’s something powerful about letting people experience your perspective, Cancer, especially when you’ve spent so much time keeping your best ideas to yourself. 

As Scorpio Season enters its final week, the Aquarius Moon activates your intimacy and shared-resources zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for tackling practical matters involving joint finances, subscriptions, or financial commitments. Then, when the moon enters fellow Water sign Pisces on the 17th, your appetite for adventure grows. You may feel inspired to research a destination you’ve always wanted to visit, explore a new neighborhood, or connect with someone from a different cultural background. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your career sector, giving you the courage to take a professional risk. Whether you’re pitching yourself for an opportunity, reaching out to a potential mentor, or announcing an exciting project, don’t underestimate how far a little initiative could take you. The spotlight looks good on you, Cancer.

Leo Sun & Rising:

Leo, the cosmic traffic jam is finally clearing, and you’re ready to get back in the driver’s seat. With Mercury now direct in your home zone and Venus moving forward in your communication realm, the first full week of both planets being direct brings a welcome sense of ease to your everyday interactions. You may find yourself laughing more with relatives, making exciting plans with siblings, or finally enjoying a living space you’ve spent weeks trying to organize. This could also be a great time to host a dinner party, explore a new neighborhood, or invite someone over who’s been asking to see you. After all the retrograde back-and-forth, there’s something refreshing about making plans without needing a Plan B, C, and D. Let yourself enjoy the simpler pleasures of life, Leo. 

As Scorpio Season enters its final stretch, the Aquarius Moon highlights your partnership zone, making the beginning of the week ideal for quality time with someone special or an exciting one-on-one collaboration. Then, when the Moon enters Pisces on the 17th, your intimacy realm gets activated, encouraging deeper conversations about your desires, finances, or future plans. By the weekend, the Aries Moon lights up your travel and adventure zone, and with Mars in your sign, you may feel an irresistible  urge to get out of town, try something spontaneous, or say yes to an experience you’d usually overthink. A last-minute getaway or an unexpected invitation could be exactly the change of scenery you need. 

Virgo Sun & Rising:

Congratulations, Virgo — your ruling planet Mercury is finally behaving again! With  Mercury moving forward in Scorpio and Venus direct in Libra, the first full week of both planets being direct could bring a noticeable improvement to your communication and financial affairs. Maybe an overdue payment finally arrives, a client responds to your proposal, or a conversation that previously went in circles suddenly becomes productive. You may also feel more confident promoting your work, reaching out to potential customers, or sharing your expertise with people who could benefit from it. If you’ve been considering teaching a class, offering a service, or monetizing a skill, this is an encouraging time to test the waters. title: I’m Sorry, But These Faux Christmas Trees Are Too Cute
text:
I’m Sorry, But These Faux Christmas Trees Are Too Cute I have a confession to make: I've been thinking about cheating on my Christmas tree this year. Not with another full-sized fir, but with a growing collection of miniature, colorful, and delightfully unconventional alternatives that have absolutely no business being this cute. And judging by the number of faux trees currently occupying my online shopping carts, this might be getting out of hand.

Don't get me wrong. I love traditional Christmas trees as much as the next person (and there are some ahead!). The twinkling lights, the sentimental ornaments, the excuse to rearrange your entire living room around a seven-foot centerpiece? I'm here for all of it. But somewhere between discovering a wicker tree dressed up in oversized velvet bows and a sparkly little number that looks like it belongs in a disco, I realized that holiday decorating doesn't have to be quite so serious.

In fact, the more personality, the better.

This year's faux Christmas trees are making a compelling case for abandoning the rule book altogether. We're talking sculptural silhouettes, unexpected textures, candy-colored branches, and designs that could easily double as art installations. Some are charmingly understated while others look like they were dreamed up by someone who considers more is more a personal philosophy. Naturally, I want both.

And here's the beauty of going faux: You can skip the falling needles, forget about watering anything, and keep your festive masterpiece looking fabulous year after year. Plus, who says you have to stop at one? A petite tree on your nightstand, a statement-making creation in the entryway, and something wonderfully ridiculous on your mantel sound like a perfectly reasonable decorating strategy to me.

Whether you're working with a tiny apartment, looking to give your usual holiday setup a little personality, or simply can't resist something shiny, I've rounded up the faux Christmas trees that deserve a spot on your nice list.

Fair warning: Your traditional tree might get a little jealous.

title: How To Gift The Ultimate Campus Capsule Wardrobe This Holiday Season
text:
How To Gift The Ultimate Campus Capsule Wardrobe This Holiday Season

We’re well into the fall and winter is on the horizon, so if you think like us, that means it’s clearly time for a wardrobe refresh. And if you or someone you know and love is on campus completing midterms, a closet pick-me-up is the perfect holiday gift! Think: a fun new sneaker or a cozy quarter zip. But with limited dorm space, a capsule wardrobe is the best bet to make the most of your clothes throughout the semester. Luckily, Nike is a one-stop shop for versatile staples that’ll take you from class presentations to football games and sorority events.

Nike’s holiday offerings has tons of hidden gems (no, it’s not all activewear!) that are ready to be carted up and shown off around campus. Ahead, we share some steps and tricks to build a campus capsule wardrobe that makes your day-to-day outfits easier to put together. That includes prioritizing comfy bottoms, walking shoes, and carryall bags with the help of Nike. So scroll on, do some retail therapy, and celebrate that you’re halfway through the semester!

DashDividers_1_500x100

Step 1: Versatile Tops

First off, you’ll want some staple tops that are versatile enough to wear for multiple activities and occasions. Consider polo that can go from a class presentation to a round of pickleball with your roommates. Or try a bolder top, like a mesh long-sleeve or trendy red short-sleeve that can be worn to the gym or styled for a sorority party.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Step 2: Comfy Bottoms

Next step, get some no-fuss, no-muss bottoms to round out every type of outfit. And they must be comfy enough to wear for long days. Beyond a pair of Nike biker shorts or track shorts, the retailer also sells cozy wide-leg sweatpants, preppy drawstring joggers, and flowy trousers that effortlessly get you from point a to point b.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Step 3: Cozy Layers

It’s time to cart up a layering piece that’s not too light and not too heavy but jussst right, aka a fall jacket. From classic barn jackets for slightly windy or rainy days to chunky fleece quarter zips and crewnecks for chillier temps, look to Nike for it all. These sleek designs are the perfect statements for “the jacket is the outfit” season.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Step 4: Walking Shoes

You’ll need a good pair of shoes to trek across campus semester after semester, so it only makes sense to invest in a new pair of Nike sneakers. Of course, there’s the classic Nike Cortez (a personal favorite). But you can also experiment with a bolder shoe, like a retro metallic sneaker with thick soles extra comfort or the Lahar Low retro trail shoe design that’s a bit more elevated (think of it as a loafer alternative!).

DashDividers_1_500x100

Step 5: Carryall Bags

If you don’t already own a backpack, you may notice the uneven back and shoulder pain that comes with lugging textbooks across campus. The solution? Well, a backpack, from a large utility style with tons of compartments to a mini puffy design for lighter class days. Nike also sells tons of stylish crossbody bags and totes that can comfortably carry your belongings to the dining hall, sporting events, field trips, and more.

DashDividers_1_500x100

Step 6: Extra Activewear

Whether you’re on a school sports team, enjoy working out to de-stress between classes, or want to be on-theme for pep rallies, you’ll want to own some activewear staples. Nike’s back-to-school selection includes sportswear across many categories, but we’re eyeing the tennis skirts and tennis dresses as well as the many longline sports bras, which can double as tank tops. And of course, you can never have too many socks, especially in cute fall colorways.
